For something so admired, so synonymous with merit, the concept of intelligence is remarkably
poorly understood. Our society operates on the assumption that people with greater intelligence
deserve access to better schools and better jobs. Many people believe that animals with higher
intelligence deserve to be treated more humanely, or at least not used for food. Our tech leaders
obsess over comparing human intelligence with the latest AI systems. Many claim that once
these systems surpass us in intelligence, they will quickly enslave us, destroy us, or solve all
our problems.


How can we compare human and machine intelligence when we can’t decide which species —
cats or dogs — is more intelligent? Scientists who study human or animal behavior and
brainpower tend to view intelligence differently, breaking it down into abilities they can
actually measure. What impressed them was a recent paper providing experimental evidence
that chimpanzees can use reasoning to weigh different strengths of evidence, draw rational
conclusions, update beliefs, and recognize the strengths and weaknesses of their own
knowledge.


This finding refutes centuries of philosophy that equated reason with human uniqueness, but it
makes sense in evolutionary terms, given our relationship to chimps and the understanding that
human traits were inherited and shaped by natural selection rather than bestowed by gods. “It’s
the strongest evidence yet that we share the planet with another rational being,” said Duke
University evolutionary anthropologist Brian Hare, who praised the new research in a
commentary piece for Science. The significance isn’t about measuring the amount of chimp
intelligence, but in understanding how our animal relatives think.

For several years, social media has been fascinated by an extraordinary presence: A petite
elderly lady with cropped grey hair, speaking in mesmerising Urdu. Her speech was pellucid,
her words measured, she talked about the beauty of language and our composite culture, of
human dignity and compassion, and of women’s rights, in ways few had heard before. Her
name was Arfa Sayeda Zehra, and she passed away in Lahore on Monday, leaving behind a
legacy that will endure far beyond her years.


Arfa Apa, as I (and many others) called her, represented a rare breed — the last of a generation
that exemplified the very best of our shared cultural heritage. I remember, years ago, having a
conversation with her at a literature festival. At some point in our discussion, I asked her to
answer a basic question: What is Urdu? She paused momentarily, and with a twinkle in her eye
as if she was about to let me in on a secret, said: “Urdu is not just a language, it is an entire
culture.”. A complete culture is not just speech but a lived experience, the sum of how one
lives, thinks, feels, and navigates the world, and it was this wholeness she dedicated her entire
life to protecting. This conviction was evident in virtually every statement she made, often with
disarming wit. Of the impossibility of translating cultural experience, she would say: “the joy
of kofta can never be experienced in meatballs.”


An uncompromising champion of women’s rights, Arfa Apa was a fearless critic of
authoritarian regimes, shaping the political landscape of her homeland. She would refer to
General Ziaul Haq as mere mehboob (“my beloved”), reminding her people that humour can
inflict deeper wounds than anger. Above all, she was a thinker who married tradition with
critique, and insisted that culture is not a static legacy, but a dynamic territory. In an era of
vanishing grace, she personified the values we are at risk of losing.

The World Health Organization’s Global Tuberculosis Report 2025 was a mixed bag for India.
While the tuberculosis (TB) incidence had the highest decline rate, globally, by 21% from 237
per lakh population in 2015 to 187 per lakh population in 2024, India remains among the
countries with the highest rates of TB, bearing 25% of the world’s burden. As far as multidrug-
resistant TB (MDR-TB) is concerned, the scenario seems quite daunting. India, as per the
report, also recorded the highest number of drug-resistant TB cases in 2024 — accounting for
32% of global MDR-TB- and rifampicin-resistant (RR-TB) cases. With a treatment success
rate for new and treated cases hovering at 90%, and at 77% for MDR-/RR-TB cases started on
second line treatment, the saga of the mixed bag continues. India’s TB mortality rate dropped
from 28 deaths per one lakh population in 2015 to 21 deaths per one lakh population in 2024.
Despite this improvement, the figure remains over three times the government’s elimination
target.


India has missed the target it set for itself, having advanced for itself the aim to eliminate TB
— by 2025, five years before the global target of 2030. While incremental gains have not
shored up to a dramatic result, this indeed has meant several million lives saved over the years.
In this then, there is hope for a successful TB control programme in a country that has been
battling TB for decades. Among the factors that have contributed to the gains include:
harnessing advanced technologies, including AI and newer tools for molecular diagnosis and
rapid detection of infection and resistance, facilitating better nutrition to prevent TB in
susceptible populations, a scheme tailored to address drug-resistant forms of TB and the
introduction of newer therapies (including BPaLM). The National TB Elimination Programme
has set itself on a progressive path for the future, but unless crucial issues such as gaps in
diagnosis (particularly in rural areas), taking care of stark socio-economic disparities and the
high MDR-/RR-TB case burden, frequent drug shortages and looming malnutrition, are
addressed with vigour, Indian efforts will continue to stay in the realm of swing and miss.

Nowhere in the democratic world, barring India, are owners forced to scrap old vehicles. In
Berlin or London, you can drive your car as long as it passes regular fitness tests, which are
strict. But in Delhi, your petrol vehicle is legally dead the day it turns 15 – diesels die at age
10. This is the state trying to protect citizens from themselves – from the emissions of their
vehicles. Well-intentioned, but without a scientific basis.


Now, a Delhi Technological University (DTU) study questions the assumed correlation
between vehicle age and emissions. It says mileage – kilometres run – affects emissions more:
“Mileage is equally important and, in many cases, more reflective of how a vehicle behaves on
the road.” Why? Because ignition systems, catalytic converters and combustion efficiency
degrade with use. Global energy and infra consultancy Ricardo had earlier shown that even
Euro 3 cars, made during 2000-04, had good emissions till a mileage of 100,000km. This year,
Polish researchers showed emissions from cars driven 86,000-160,000km were significantly
higher than those for low-mileage cars. The takeaway from all rigorous research is that mileage
matters more than age.


Given that Delhi govt has challenged the vehicle age-based scrappage policy in SC, these points
deserve attention. Indiscriminate – without regard to actual condition – scrapping of vehicles
has a huge environmental cost, because making new cars consumes materials and energy. You
may recycle the steel and aluminium, but the plastics – dashboards, door panels, etc – can only
be ‘downcycled’. The electronics – old chips, music systems, etc – are sheer waste, and so are
the tyres, batteries, engine fluids. Above all, mandatory scrapping is an impost on owners.
What the state didn’t give, it mustn’t take away without a compelling reason, which, judging
by the evidence, doesn’t exist.

A recent review of National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test-Undergraduate (NEET-UG) 2025
reveals a troubling pattern: even in a relatively cheating scandal-free year, the exam system is
still tripping over basic failures. Across multiple states, an internal government assessment
found non-functional CCTVs, poor coverage of strong rooms, and invigilation lapses in exam
centres. Some had cameras positioned so poorly, they might as well not have existed. Others
had more than half their systems down. In several locations, monitoring teams couldn't even
log into portals to view real-time footage. These are not sophisticated breaches, but routine,
fixable operational gaps. And that's what makes them so worrying.


For an exam that determines the future of lakhs of students, these are bare-minimum
safeguards. If India genuinely wants to dismantle the education factory racket - coaching
dependency, retesting spiral, question paper leakage ecosystem - then the basics must work.
Every glitch erodes trust among those students who do things the right way without resorting
to 'shortcuts', who slog for years, and who can't afford to drop a year because it's too expensive
for their families to reinvest. For them, a compromised exam isn't just heartbreaking, it's
categorically exclusionary. It quietly pushes out deserving candidates who depend on a fair,
predictable system to rise.


The education ministry has now told the National Testing Agency (NTA) to rebuild CCTV
systems, fix camera placement, ensure uninterrupted live feeds and enforce tougher oversight
for 2026. Unless India gets these basics right, degrees awarded in an already hyperactive,
overcrowded job market will be worthless. An exam needs to test candidates. Not bypass it by
merely passing them.

by the President of India usually in the month of March/April every year where the awardees
are presented a Sanad (certificate) signed by the President and a medallion. The recipients are

payable only out of distributable profits; if the company does not earn profits, no dividend
obligation accrues. Since redemption of preference shares is legally permissible only when the
company has distributable profits or proceeds from a fresh issue of shares, the failure to redeem
in the absence of profits does not constitute a legal default.

not contrary to the indemnifier's instructions and was one a prudent person would have made.

The critical structural distinction between a contract of indemnity and a contract of guarantee
lies in the nature of the underlying liability. A guarantor's liability is secondary: the guarantor
becomes liable only upon the default of the principal debtor, and the very existence of a primary
obligor is an essential feature of the guarantee structure. An indemnifier's liability, by contrast,
is primary and independent: it does not depend on the existence or default of a third party. The
indemnified party can proceed directly against the indemnifier upon occurrence of the
stipulated loss, without first pursuing any other party.

Courts have recognised the principle of anticipatory indemnity, which holds that an
indemnified party need not wait until an actual loss is suffered to invoke the contract. Where a
loss is imminent or where the indemnified party has been made subject to an enforceable
liability, such as a binding court decree, the indemnifier's obligation to pay crystallises at that
point, before actual disbursement occurs. This principle prevents the inequity of requiring the
indemnified party to discharge the liability from its own funds before it can claim
reimbursement. Separately, claims for contractual damages under Section 73 of the ICA, which
require proof of actual, contemplated loss flowing from breach, operate differently from
indemnity claims, which are governed by the specific terms of the indemnity agreement and
the loss event defined within it.

The doctrine of separation of powers is a foundational constitutional principle that distributes
legislative, executive, and judicial functions among the three organs of the State. In India,
Parliament holds plenary legislative power to enact, amend, and repeal laws under the
Constitution; the judiciary is empowered to interpret those laws and to adjudicate disputes.
These functions are distinct: while courts may read down unconstitutional provisions or fill
limited interpretive gaps in legislation, they may not, in the exercise of their jurisdiction, create
new criminal offences, expand the categories of prohibited conduct, or prescribe punishments
for acts not already proscribed by statute.

In Ashwini Kumar Upadhyay v. Union of India (2026 SCC OnLine SC 741), the Supreme
Court dismissed a writ petition seeking directions to the Union Government to enact legislation
criminalising hate speech and rumour-mongering. The Court held that the existing statutory
framework, including provisions in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 prohibiting promotion
of enmity between groups, insulting religious beliefs, and disturbing public tranquility,
adequately addresses acts that meet the threshold of criminal hate speech. No 'legislative
vacuum' existed that would justify judicial intervention.

The Court expressly distinguished the conditions under which it had previously issued
guidelines with quasi-legislative character. In Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), directions
on workplace sexual harassment were issued because there was a complete absence of
legislation on the subject, creating a vacuum that violated the State's constitutional obligations.
The Court in Upadhyay held that this rationale is narrow and exceptional: judicial lawmaking
in the criminal sphere is foreclosed even where existing legislation may be imperfect or
unenforced. The Constitution assigns the judgment of what ought to be criminal to Parliament,
and courts must defer to that allocation, issuing only interpretive rulings, not legislative
mandates, even when confronted with urgent social concerns.

The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) consolidates and modernises the law
governing the admissibility of electronic and digital records in Indian courts, replacing the
corresponding provisions of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. Section 61 of the BSA contains a
non-obstante clause providing that electronic records shall not be denied admission in evidence
solely on the ground that they are in electronic form. The effect of this provision is to place
electronic records on a par with documentary records, subject to conditions of authenticity and
integrity rather than mode of existence.

Section 63 of the BSA sets out the conditions for the admissibility of output produced by a
computer or other electronic device. The key requirement is certification: a printout or other
computer output must be accompanied by a certificate issued by a responsible official with
knowledge of the computer system, typically the person in charge of the device or the relevant
part of the system, and, separately, a certificate from an expert in computer operations. This
dual certificate requirement is designed to ensure both operational authenticity and technical
integrity of the output. Where electronic records are stored using hash-based verification
methods, in which the electronic document is assigned a unique alphanumeric identifier that
changes if the document is altered, a certificate verifying the hash value constitutes strong
evidence of integrity.

The BSA draws a deliberate distinction between the admissibility of a record and the weight to
be accorded to it. Section 63 compliance speaks primarily to the threshold question of
admissibility: once the conditions are satisfied, the record enters evidence. Subsequent
questions of reliability, accuracy, and credibility, including whether the system was operating
correctly, whether the output represents what it purports to represent, and whether tampering
occurred, are matters for the court's evaluation in the context of the overall evidence. The party
seeking to rely on the electronic record bears the initial burden of satisfying the certification
requirements; once admitted, the opponent may challenge its weight.

The debate over minimum wage policy is one of the most persistent in economics. Proponents
argue that raising the minimum wage is the most direct way to improve living standards for the
lowest-paid workers, giving them more money to spend and thereby stimulating local
economies. Critics, on the other hand, contend that artificially raising the price of labour forces
employers to hire fewer workers, ultimately hurting the very people the policy intends to help.
For decades, these two positions seemed irreconcilable, each backed by theoretical models that
predicted opposite outcomes.

More recent empirical research has complicated the picture. A landmark study by economists
David Card and Alan Krueger in the early 1990s compared employment levels in fast-food
restaurants in New Jersey, where the minimum wage had just been raised, with those in
neighbouring Pennsylvania, where it had not. Contrary to what standard theory predicted,
employment in New Jersey did not fall — it actually rose slightly. This finding was
controversial, but subsequent studies in multiple countries have broadly supported the
conclusion that moderate minimum wage increases do not cause significant job losses in most
labour markets.

The reason, economists now suggest, is that labour markets do not behave like simple
commodity markets. Many employers have significant “monopsony power” — meaning they
face limited competition for workers in a given area and can therefore pay wages below the
competitive rate. A minimum wage, in this context, corrects a market failure rather than
creating one. However, critics of large, rapid minimum wage increases point out that the Card-
Krueger study involved a modest increase, and that the relationship may not hold when wages
are raised dramatically, particularly for small businesses with thin profit margins.

Policymakers who treat the minimum wage as a blunt instrument, applying the same rate across
